Jeremiah 1: Jeremiah, a priest from Anathoth in Benjamin, is called "in the thirteenth year" of Josiah (Jeremiah 1:2), 627 BC. His ministry runs to Jerusalem's fall in 586 BC and beyond.
Jeremiah 2: The early oracles, from Josiah's reign, recall Israel's wilderness years and condemn reliance on Egypt and Assyria (Jeremiah 2:18).
Jeremiah 3: "In the days of Josiah" (Jeremiah 3:6), Jeremiah compares Judah with northern Israel, which Assyria had already taken in 722 BC.
Jeremiah 4: Jeremiah warns of an invader "from the north" (Jeremiah 4:6) and calls for trumpets in Judah and Jerusalem.
Jeremiah 5: Jeremiah is told to search Jerusalem's streets for one man who does justly.
Jeremiah 6: The warning of an army from the north continues, with trumpets in Tekoa and signals in Bethhaccerem (Jeremiah 6:1).
Jeremiah 7: Jeremiah stands "in the gate of the LORD's house" (Jeremiah 7:2) and warns that the temple will become like Shiloh. Jeremiah 26 places the same message early in Jehoiakim's reign, about 609 BC.
Jeremiah 8: The bones of Judah's kings and priests will be taken from their graves. The chapter mentions a balm in Gilead (Jeremiah 8:22), an aromatic resin traded from east of the Jordan.
Jeremiah 9: Jeremiah weeps over Jerusalem and calls for the mourning women (Jeremiah 9:17), professional mourners at funerals.
Jeremiah 10: Jeremiah contrasts the LORD with idols made by craftsmen and covered with silver from Tarshish and gold from Uphaz (Jeremiah 10:9). Verse 11 is written in Aramaic.
Jeremiah 11: Jeremiah proclaims "the words of this covenant" (Jeremiah 11:2) and learns of a plot against him by the men of Anathoth, his hometown.
Jeremiah 12: Jeremiah asks why the wicked prosper; the reply mentions "the swelling of Jordan" (Jeremiah 12:5), its thick riverside jungle.
Jeremiah 13: Jeremiah buries a linen girdle by the Euphrates (Hebrew Perath) and later finds it ruined (Jeremiah 13:4–7). The king and queen mother are named in Jeremiah 13:18.
Jeremiah 14: A severe drought dries up Judah's cisterns and fields (Jeremiah 14:1–6).
Jeremiah 15: God says Judah's fate is sealed "because of Manasseh" (Jeremiah 15:4), the king who reigned fifty-five years.
Jeremiah 16: Jeremiah is told not to marry or have children, or to join funerals or feasts, as signs of coming judgment.
Jeremiah 17: Jeremiah stands in the gates of Jerusalem and warns against carrying burdens on the sabbath (Jeremiah 17:19–22).
Jeremiah 18: Jeremiah watches a potter at work on the wheels (Jeremiah 18:3).
Jeremiah 19: Jeremiah breaks a clay bottle in the valley of the son of Hinnom, by the east gate (Jeremiah 19:2), where children had been sacrificed at Tophet.
Jeremiah 20: Pashur, the chief governor of the temple, puts Jeremiah in the stocks by the high gate of Benjamin (Jeremiah 20:1–2).
Jeremiah 21: King Zedekiah sends to Jeremiah as Nebuchadnezzar attacks Jerusalem (Jeremiah 21:1–2), about 588 BC.
Jeremiah 22: Jeremiah addresses the kings who followed Josiah: Shallum (Jehoahaz), taken to Egypt, Jehoiakim, and Coniah (Jehoiachin).
Jeremiah 23: Jeremiah promises a righteous Branch for David and condemns the false prophets of Samaria and Jerusalem.
Jeremiah 24: After Jeconiah is taken to Babylon in 597 BC (Jeremiah 24:1), Jeremiah sees two baskets of figs before the temple.
Jeremiah 25: In the fourth year of Jehoiakim, the first year of Nebuchadnezzar (Jeremiah 25:1), 605 BC, Jeremiah predicts seventy years of Babylonian rule.
Jeremiah 26: "In the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim" (Jeremiah 26:1), about 609 BC, Jeremiah's temple sermon nearly costs him his life. The prophet Urijah is killed for a similar message.
Jeremiah 27: Envoys from Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon come to Zedekiah in Jerusalem (Jeremiah 27:3), apparently planning revolt. Jeremiah wears a yoke as a sign to submit to Babylon.
Jeremiah 28: In Zedekiah's fourth year, the fifth month (Jeremiah 28:1), 594 BC, the prophet Hananiah breaks Jeremiah's yoke and dies within the year.
Jeremiah 29: Jeremiah writes to the exiles in Babylon, taken in 597 BC, telling them to build houses and plant gardens there.
Jeremiah 30: Jeremiah is told to write in a book God's promise to bring back the captivity of Israel and Judah (Jeremiah 30:2–3).
Jeremiah 31: The promise of return includes Rachel weeping in Ramah (Jeremiah 31:15), a town north of Jerusalem where exiles were gathered (Jeremiah 40:1).
Jeremiah 32: In Zedekiah's tenth year, 587 BC, with Babylon besieging Jerusalem and Jeremiah imprisoned, he buys a field at Anathoth and seals the deed in an earthen jar (Jeremiah 32:1–14).
Jeremiah 33: While Jeremiah is still "shut up in the court of the prison" (Jeremiah 33:1), God promises restoration.
Jeremiah 34: During the siege, when only Lachish and Azekah still hold out (Jeremiah 34:7), Zedekiah frees the Hebrew slaves, and the owners take them back.
Jeremiah 35: "In the days of Jehoiakim" (Jeremiah 35:1), the Rechabites, who drink no wine and live in tents, have taken refuge in Jerusalem from Babylon's army.
Jeremiah 36: In Jehoiakim's fourth year, 605 BC, Baruch writes Jeremiah's words in a scroll. In the ninth month, Jehoiakim burns it piece by piece in his winter house (Jeremiah 36:1, 22–23).
Jeremiah 37: The Babylonian siege lifts briefly when Pharaoh's army comes out of Egypt (Jeremiah 37:5), about 588 BC. Jeremiah is arrested as a deserter.
Jeremiah 38: Jeremiah is lowered into the dungeon of Malchiah and sinks in the mire, until Ebedmelech the Ethiopian rescues him (Jeremiah 38:6–13).
Jeremiah 39: Jerusalem falls on the ninth day of the fourth month of Zedekiah's eleventh year (Jeremiah 39:2), 586 BC. Nebuchadnezzar's officers free Jeremiah.
Jeremiah 40: Nebuzaradan releases Jeremiah at Ramah, and he joins Gedaliah, whom Babylon made governor, at Mizpah.
Jeremiah 41: In the seventh month, Ishmael son of Nethaniah murders Gedaliah at Mizpah (Jeremiah 41:1–2).
Jeremiah 42: The remaining Judeans ask Jeremiah whether to go to Egypt; after ten days he tells them to stay.
Jeremiah 43: The people go to Egypt anyway, taking Jeremiah and Baruch, as far as Tahpanhes in the eastern Nile Delta (Jeremiah 43:7).
Jeremiah 44: Jeremiah speaks to Jews living at Migdol, Tahpanhes, Noph, and Pathros in Egypt (Jeremiah 44:1). They burn incense to "the queen of heaven."
Jeremiah 45: A message to Baruch son of Neriah, Jeremiah's scribe, dated to Jehoiakim's fourth year (Jeremiah 45:1), 605 BC, when Baruch wrote the scroll of Jeremiah 36.
Jeremiah 46: The oracle against Egypt begins with Pharaoh Necho's defeat at Carchemish on the Euphrates in Jehoiakim's fourth year (Jeremiah 46:2), 605 BC.
Jeremiah 47: The oracle against the Philistines is dated "before that Pharaoh smote Gaza" (Jeremiah 47:1).
Jeremiah 48: The oracle against Moab names many of its towns, including Nebo, Kiriathaim, Heshbon, Dibon, and Kerioth.
Jeremiah 49: Oracles against Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar, Hazor, and Elam follow. The Elam oracle is dated to the beginning of Zedekiah's reign (Jeremiah 49:34).
Jeremiah 50: The oracle against Babylon names its god Bel and Merodach (Marduk) (Jeremiah 50:2). Babylon fell to Cyrus of Persia in 539 BC.
Jeremiah 51: The oracle against Babylon is sent with Seraiah when he goes to Babylon with Zedekiah in his fourth year (Jeremiah 51:59), 594 BC.
Jeremiah 52: An account of Jerusalem's fall like 2 Kings 25 closes the book. It ends with Jehoiachin freed in the thirty-seventh year of his captivity (Jeremiah 52:31), about 562 BC; Babylonian ration tablets list rations for ‘Yaukin, king of Judah.’
Lamentations 1: The five poems mourn Jerusalem after Babylon destroyed it in 586 BC. Tradition credits Jeremiah, who lamented Josiah (2 Chronicles 35:25); the book does not name its author.
Lamentations 2: The second poem describes the temple's destruction and the king and princes "among the Gentiles" (Lamentations 2:9).
Lamentations 3: The third poem is spoken by one man who has suffered: "I am the man that hath seen affliction" (Lamentations 3:1). Its sixty-six verses form a triple alphabetical acrostic.
Lamentations 4: The fourth poem describes famine in the siege and the capture of "the anointed of the LORD" (Lamentations 4:20), the king.
Lamentations 5: The fifth poem is a prayer from survivors under foreign rule: "Servants have ruled over us" (Lamentations 5:8).
